title: From a Mother's Longing to a Child's Fight for Life: Rahma and The Farm Bring Moving Stories to IFFI
subtitle: The Human Urge to Control Comes at a Cost to Other Living Beings: Elif Eda
body_text:
Posted On: 23 NOV 2026 2:21PM by PIB Mumbai Release ID: 2340295 Views: 122 A A Print Share X Facebook Instagram WhatsApp Copy Article Link
Read in: English Marathi Gujarati Kannada
Goa, 23 November 2026 Stories of motherhood, compassion, human vulnerability and the sanctity of life came into focus at a press conference featuring filmmakers associated with two films showcased under the International Cinema Section of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), being held in Goa. The films, Rahma and The Farm, explore distinct yet deeply interconnected themes, inviting audiences to look beyond their own struggles and recognise the pain and aspirations of others. The press conference was attended by Faysal Soysal, director and writer of Rahma; Elif Eda, director and writer of The Farm; and Emre Pekçakır, director of photography of The Farm. The filmmakers shared insights into the creative vision, thematic concerns and experiences behind bringing these compelling stories to the screen. Rahma: A poignant exploration of motherhood, longing and human connection Directed and written by Faysal Soysal , Rahma follows Meryem, an archaeologist whose longing to become a mother remains unfulfilled despite multiple surgeries and unsuccessful IVF treatments. As hope begins to fade, she considers surrogacy in Georgia, despite her husband İbrahim's reservations. Her life takes an unexpected turn when she encounters Rahma, a nine-year-old Syrian orphan struggling to survive on her own. As Meryem gradually discovers Rahma's situation, an extraordinary bond begins to develop between them, bringing solace and emotional healing into her life. Speaking about the inspiration behind the film, Faysal Soysal said that the story emerged from a reflection on the intense struggles couples undergo in their desire to have children, juxtaposed with the many children who grow up without families. Through Rahma, he sought to explore the emotional complexities of parenthood, the meaning of family and the unexpected ways in which human relationships can fulfil deep-seated emotional needs. The Farm: A young girl's courageous stand for the sanctity of life Written and directed by Elif Eda , The Farm tells the story of 12-year-old İrem, who moves in with her estranged grandmother on a dairy farm following the sudden loss of her parents. Disturbed by the practice of separating newborn calves from their mothers to increase milk production, İrem is unable to reconcile with the cruelty she witnesses. With the help of Halid, an orphan working as an apprentice to the farm's veterinarian, she sets out on a determined mission to free the pregnant cows. Elif Eda spoke about the central philosophy of the film, emphasising the importance of respecting all forms of life and developing empathy for the suffering of others. She observed that the real danger lies not merely in experiencing pain, but in becoming indifferent to the pain endured by others. Highlighting the sanctity of life on Earth, she reflected on how humans desire to control everything often becomes a source of suffering for other living beings. The filmmaker explained that she wanted to give a voice to the often-unseen suffering of animals through the film. She also spoke about the challenges of establishing oneself as a woman director in the film industry, highlighting the additional difficulties women encounter while pursuing their creative aspirations. Sharing his experience of working on The Farm, Director of Photography Emre Pekçakır spoke about the unique challenges he faced while filming the cows. Recalling the production experience, he said that he spent considerable time on the farms, staying close to the animals to capture their behaviour and the nuances of their surroundings. Despite the challenges, he described the experience of shooting with the animals as an enjoyable and enriching part of the filmmaking process. Together, Rahman and The Farm offer moving reflections on compassion, belonging and empathy, reminding audiences to look beyond their own circumstances and acknowledge the lives and struggles of others.
